claim: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the main challenges facing modern medicine.
source: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the main challenges facing modern medicine.
evidence: This is a statement of scientific consensus about the importance of AMR as a medical challenge.

claim: As many as 700,000 people die per year due to AMR-related problems.
source: some estimates suggest as many as 700,000 people die per year due to AMR-related problems (O'Neill et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Neill et al., 2016.

claim: The dominant mode of growth for most microbes is on surfaces.
source: The dominant mode of growth for most microbes is on surfaces
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about microbial growth.

claim: The biofilm lifestyle is central to antimicrobial resistance.
source: this biofilm lifestyle is central to AMR (Høiby et al., 2010; Olsen, 2015; Ahmed et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Biofilms are especially important in chronic infections.
source: especially in chronic infections (Wolcott et al., 2010; Wolcott, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wolcott et al., 2010 and Wolcott, 2017.

claim: Most research on the evolution of AMR has been conducted in well-mixed populations.
source: most of the research on the evolution of AMR has been conducted in well-mixed populations (reviewed in Hughes and Andersson, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a review citation.

claim: The close proximity of cells in biofilms may facilitate the horizontal transfer and persistence of resistance genes in bacterial populations.
source: the close proximity of cells in biofilms may facilitate the horizontal transfer and persistence of resistance genes in bacterial populations (Stalder and Top, 2016; Ridenhour et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and involves speculation about mechanisms.

claim: The environmental structure of biofilms can increase clonal interference, rendering selection less effective and enhancing genetic diversity.
source: the environmental structure of biofilms can increase clonal interference, rendering selection less effective and enhancing genetic diversity (Habets et al., 2006; Traverse et al., 2013; Cooper et al., 2014; Ellis et al., 2015; France et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Distinct ecological conditions within the biofilm can favor functionally distinct adaptations to different niches.
source: distinct ecological conditions within the biofilm can favor functionally distinct adaptations to different niches (Poltak and Cooper, 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: The biofilm itself can protect its residents from being exposed to external stresses like antibiotics or host immunity, and weaken selection.
source: the biofilm itself can protect its residents from being exposed to external stresses like antibiotics or host immunity, and weaken selection (Geisinger and Isberg, 2015; Eze et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Slower growth within biofilms can reduce the efficacy of antibiotics that preferentially attack fast-growing cells.
source: slower growth within biofilms can reduce the efficacy of antibiotics that preferentially attack fast-growing cells (Walters et al., 2003; Kirby et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Acinetobacter baumannii is often intrinsically resistant to antibiotics or has been reported to rapidly evolve resistance to them.
source: the opportunistic nosocomial pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii, which is often intrinsically resistant to antibiotics or has been reported to rapidly evolve resistance to them (Doi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Acinetobacter baumannii is categorized as one of the highest threats to patient safety.
source: This pathogen is categorized as one of the highest threats to patient safety (Asif et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Acinetobacter baumannii has the ability to live on inanimate surfaces in biofilms.
source: partly due to its ability to live on inanimate surfaces in biofilms (Eze et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Replicate cultures of A. baumannii strain ATCC 17978 were established under planktonic or biofilm conditions in three treatments: no antibiotics, sub-inhibitory concentration of ciprofloxacin, and evolutionary rescue with increasing CIP concentrations.
source: Replicate cultures of the susceptible A. baumannii strain ATCC 17978 (Piechaud and Second, 1951; Baumann et al., 1968) were established under planktonic or biofilm conditions in one of three treatments: i) no antibiotics, ii) sub-inhibitory concentration of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin (CIP) and iii) evolutionary rescue (Bell and Gonzalez, 2009) in which CIP concentrations were increased every 72 hr from subinhibitory concentrations to four times the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is supported by the figure reference.

claim: Before the start of the antibiotic evolution experiment, the ATCC strain was propagated for ten days in planktonic conditions to reduce the influence of adaptation to laboratory conditions.
source: Before the start of the antibiotic evolution experiment, we propagated the ATCC strain for ten days in planktonic conditions to reduce the influence of adaptation to the laboratory conditions on subsequent comparisons.
evidence: This describes a methodological step in the experimental design.

claim: CIP was chosen because of its clinical importance in treating A. baumannii.
source: CIP was chosen because of its clinical importance in treating A. baumannii (Lopes and Amyes, 2013; Ardebili et al., 2014; Doi et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: CIP has the ability to penetrate the biofilm matrix.
source: its ability to penetrate the biofilm matrix (Tseng et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: CIP allows similar efficacy in well mixed and structured populations.
source: allowing similar efficacy in well mixed and structured populations (Kirby et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: CIP is not known to stimulate biofilm formation in A. baumannii.
source: it is not known to stimulate biofilm formation in A. baumannii (Aka and Haji, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Planktonic populations became approximately 160x more resistant on average than the ancestral clone while biofilm populations became only 6x more resistant.
source: Planktonic populations became approximately 160x more resistant on average than the ancestral clone while the biofilm populations became only 6x more resistant (Figure 1B and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: Planktonic populations evolved resistance much more rapidly, becoming 10x more resistant after only 24 hr of growth in sub-inhibitory CIP.
source: Planktonic populations also evolved resistance much more rapidly, becoming 10x more resistant after only 24 hr of growth in sub-inhibitory CIP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The evolution of resistance far beyond the selective requirement indicates that mutations conferring higher resistance also increased fitness in planktonic populations exposed to CIP.
source: The evolution of resistance far beyond the selective requirement indicates that mutations conferring higher resistance also increased fitness in planktonic populations exposed to CIP.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that resistance levels exceeded what was necessary for survival.

claim: Biofilm populations evolved under the evolutionary rescue regime acquired much lower levels of resistance (ca. 3–7x the ancestral MIC) and primarily in a single step between days 3 and 4.
source: In contrast, biofilm-evolved populations evolved under the evolutionary rescue regime acquired much lower levels of resistance (ca. 3– 7x the ancestral MIC) and primarily in a single step between days 3 and 4 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: In biofilm population B2, the MIC increased ~50x after 3 days of selection in subinhibitory concentrations of CIP, but then the resistance of this population declined to only 6x higher than the ancestral strain.
source: In one notable exception, the MIC of biofilm population B2 increased ~50 x after 3 days of selection in subinhibitory concentrations of CIP (Figure 1B), but then the resistance of this population declined to only 6x higher than the ancestral strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The dynamic in biofilm population B2 suggested that a mutant conferring high-level resistance rose to intermediate frequency but was replaced by a more fit, yet less resistant, mutant.
source: This dynamic suggested that a mutant conferring high-level resistance rose to intermediate frequency but was replaced by a more fit, yet less resistant, mutant (this possibility is evaluated below).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed dynamics in population B2.

claim: Biofilm populations exposed to subinhibitory CIP were 4x more resistant than the ancestor.
source: Biofilm populations were 4x more resistant than the ancestor
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Planktonic populations exposed to subinhibitory CIP were 20x more resistant than the ancestor.
source: planktonic populations were 20x more resistant (Table 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Table 1.

claim: Biofilm growth does not select for the high-level resistance seen in planktonic populations, instead favoring mutants with low levels of resistance and better adapted to life in a biofilm.
source: We can infer that biofilm growth does not select for the high-level resistance seen in planktonic populations, instead favoring mutants with low levels of resistance and better adapted to life in a biofilm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed differences in resistance levels between biofilm and planktonic populations.

claim: MIC measurements increased when measured in biofilm compared to planktonic conditions.
source: It is important to note that these MIC measurements were made in planktonic conditions according to the clinical standards (CLSI, 2019) and that these values increased when measured in biofilm (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: Clinical isolates producing more biofilm were less resistant than non-biofilm-forming isolates.
source: Our results correspond with studies of clinical isolates in which those producing more biofilm (and likely having adapted in biofilm conditions) were less resistant than non-biofilm-forming isolates (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Exposing bacteria to low levels of antibiotic risks selection for high levels of resistance that can make future treatment more difficult.
source: Overall, the fact that the planktonic populations exposed to subinhibitory concentrations of CIP increased their resistance level approximately 20-fold (Table 1) demonstrates that exposing bacteria to low levels of antibiotic risks selection for high levels of resistance that can make future treatment more difficult (Wistrand-Yuen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation.

claim: In large bacterial populations growing under strong selection, adaptive mutations conferring beneficial traits such as antibiotic resistance will dominate population dynamics.
source: In large bacterial populations (>105 cells) growing under strong selection, adaptive mutations conferring beneficial traits such as antibiotic resistance will dominate population dynamics (Barrick and Lenski, 2013; Cooper, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A conservative estimate of 106 mutations occur in the first growth cycle and at least 107 mutations arise over the 12 days of selection.
source: a conservative estimate of 106 mutations occur in the first growth cycle and at least 107 mutations arise over the 12 days of selection, leading to a probability of 0.98 that every site in the 4Mbp A. baumannii genome experiences a mutation at least once over the course of the 12 day experiment (see Supplementary file 1 for details of these calculations)
evidence: This claim is based on calculations detailed in supplementary materials.

claim: High nonsynonymous to synonymous mutation ratios were observed in both lifestyles (8.5 in planktonic and 9.7 in biofilm).
source: High nonsynonymous to synonymous mutation ratios were observed in both lifestyles (8.5 in planktonic and 9.7 in biofilm).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: 43% of the total mutations in planktonic and 34% in biofilm were insertions or deletions.
source: 43% of the total mutations in planktonic and 34% in biofilm were insertions or deletions, which is vastly enriched over typical mutation rates of ~10 SNPs/indel under neutral conditions (Lynch et al., 2016; Dillon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and citations.

claim: Roughly 30% of the mutations in CIP-treated populations of either lifestyle occurred in intergenic regions, which is statistically enriched over the approximately 13.5% of intergenic regions of the ancestral strain.
source: Roughly 30% of the mutations in CIP-treated populations of either lifestyle occurred in intergenic regions, which is statistically enriched over the approximately 13.5% of intergenic regions of the ancestral strain (X-squared = 8.2237, df = 2, p-value=0.01638).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and statistical analysis.

claim: 72% of the planktonic intergenic mutations and 18% of the biofilm intergenic mutations occurred in promoters, 5' untranslated regions, sRNAs or in putative terminators.
source: Of the intergenic mutations, 72% of the planktonic mutations and 18% of the biofilm mutations occurred in promoters, 5' untranslated regions, sRNAs or in putative terminators (Kröger et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and a citation.

claim: In CIP-selected planktonic populations, one or two mutations rapidly outcompeted others and fixed.
source: As expected from theory, in CIP-selected planktonic populations where selection is most efficient, one or two mutations rapidly outcompeted others and fixed (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Selection in biofilms produced fewer selective sweeps and maintained more contending mutations, especially at lower antibiotic concentrations.
source: Selection in biofilms, however, produced fewer selective sweeps and maintained more contending mutations, especially at lower antibiotic concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: Biofilm-adapted populations were significantly more diverse than the planktonic-adapted populations across all treatments and timepoints.
source: Overall, across all treatments and timepoints, biofilm-adapted populations were significantly more diverse than the planktonic-adapted populations (Shannon index; Kruskal Wallis, chi-squared = 7.723, p=0.005), particularly at subinhibitory concentrations of CIP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and figure reference.

claim: Increasing drug concentrations eliminated the differences in diversity between treatments.
source: Notably, increasing drug concentrations eliminated the differences in diversity between treatments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Drug-free control populations contained no mutations that achieved high frequency during the experiment.
source: In contrast with the data observed in the populations evolving under CIP pressure, drug-free control populations contained no mutations that achieved high frequency during the experiment (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The ancestral starting clone was already well adapted both to planktonic and biofilm lifestyles.
source: These results suggest that the ancestral starting clone was already well adapted both to planktonic and biofilm lifestyles, likely because we had previously propagated the A. baumannii ATCC 17978 clone under identical drug-free conditions for 10 days leading to the fixation of mutations in three genes (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of high-frequency mutations in drug-free controls.

claim: A. baumannii clinical samples acquire resistance to CIP by two principal mechanisms: modification of the direct antibiotic targets or by the overexpression of efflux pumps.
source: A. baumannii clinical samples acquire resistance to CIP by two principal mechanisms: modification of the direct antibiotic targets — gyrase A or B and topoisomerase IV — or by the overexpression of efflux pumps reducing the intracellular concentrations of the antibiotic (Doi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Mutations disrupting three negative regulators of efflux pumps evolved in parallel across populations exposed to CIP.
source: Mutations disrupting three negative regulators of efflux pumps evolved in parallel across populations exposed to CIP
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: Mutations in adeL and adeS were nearly exclusive to biofilm clones.
source: but mutations in two of these (adeL and adeS) were nearly exclusive to biofilm clones (Figure 2E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The most common and highest frequency mutations observed in the biofilm populations were in the repressor gene adeL.
source: The most common and highest frequency mutations observed in the biofilm populations were in the repressor gene adeL (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Table 4)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures and tables.

claim: adeL regulates AdeFGH, one of three resistance-nodulation-division (RND) efflux pump systems in A. baumannii.
source: which regulates AdeFGH, one of three resistance-nodulation-division (RND) efflux pump systems in A. baumannii (Coyne et al., 2010; Fernando et al., 2013; Pournaras et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The overexpression of the AdeFGH is predicted to enhance transport of acylated homoserine lactones, which can increase both biofilm and antibiotic resistance.
source: The overexpression of the AdeFGH is predicted to enhance transport of acylated homoserine lactones, which can increase both biofilm and antibiotic resistance (He et al., 2015; Alav et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: In the planktonic lines, the predominant mutations were found in adeN, which is a negative regulator of AdeIJK.
source: In the planktonic lines, the predominant mutations were found in adeN, which is a negative regulator of AdeIJK and were mainly insertions of IS701 that disrupted the gene (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data and a citation.

claim: AdeIJK contributes to resistance to biocides, hospital disinfectants, and to both intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance in A. baumannii.
source: AdeIJK contributes to resistance to biocides, hospital disinfectants, and to both intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance in A. baumannii (Damier-Piolle et al., 2008; Rosenfeld et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: AdeIJK may decrease biofilm formation.
source: and may decrease biofilm formation, which could explain its prevalence in planktonic populations here (Yoon et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and involves inference about the mechanism.

claim: In biofilm lines, different contending adeL mutations were detected in each replicate after 24 hr then eventually fixed as CIP concentrations increased.
source: In biofilm lines, different contending adeL mutations were detected in each replicate after 24 hr then eventually fixed as CIP concentrations increased (green lines in Figure 2B)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Altering efflux via adeL generates adaptations to the combination of CIP and biofilm which is supported by the increase in biofilm formation by the adeL mutants.
source: This pattern suggests that altering efflux via adeL generates adaptations to the combination of CIP and biofilm which is supported by the increase in biofilm formation by the adeL mutants (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mutants with higher resistance than necessary appear to be maladaptive in the biofilm treatment.
source: Further, mutants with higher resistance than necessary appear to be maladaptive in the biofilm treatment.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed dynamics in biofilm populations.

claim: All planktonic populations with increasing concentrations of CIP eventually underwent selective sweeps of a single high frequency mutation in gyrA (S81L).
source: In contrast to the biofilm populations, all planktonic populations with increasing concentrations of CIP eventually underwent selective sweeps of a single high frequency mutation in gyrA (S81L), the canonical ciprofloxacin-resistant mutation in DNA gyrase.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: gyrA mutations evolved in genetic backgrounds containing either an adeN mutant or a pgpB mutant.
source: These gyrA mutations evolved in genetic backgrounds containing either an adeN mutant or a pgpB mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: pgpB is a gene that encodes a putative membrane associated lipid phosphatase and is co-regulated by adeN.
source: pgpB is a gene that encodes a putative membrane associated lipid phosphatase and is co-regulated by adeN (Hua et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Bacterial lifestyle influences the evolutionary dynamics and targets of selection of AMR.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that bacterial lifestyle influences the evolutionary dynamics and targets of selection of AMR.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: adeN mutations decrease biofilm formation and increase resistance by altering the adeN-controlled adeIJK efflux pump.
source: For instance, adeN mutations decrease biofilm formation and increase resistance by altering the adeN-controlled adeIJK efflux pump (Yoon et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in regulators of the adeFGH and adeABC RND efflux pumps were selected in CIP-treated biofilm populations and increased resistance ~4 fold.
source: In contrast, loss-of-function mutations in regulators of the adeFGH and adeABC RND efflux pumps were selected in CIP-treated biofilm populations and increased resistance ~4 fold
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: A longstanding hypothesis is that de novo acquired antibiotic resistance is associated with a fitness cost in the absence of antibiotics.
source: A longstanding hypothesis is that de novo acquired antibiotic resistance is associated with a fitness cost in the absence of antibiotics (reviewed in Vogwill and MacLean, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a review citation.

claim: A negative correlation between CIP resistance and fitness of resistant genotypes in the absence of antibiotics has been previously described in Escherichia coli.
source: A negative correlation between CIP resistance and fitness of resistant genotypes in the absence of antibiotics has been previously described in Escherichia coli, suggesting a trade-off between these traits (Marcusson et al., 2009; Huseby et al., 2017; Basra et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Biofilm clones were much less resistant in planktonic conditions than those evolved planktonically.
source: As expected from the population mean values (Figure 1B), the biofilm clones much were less resistant in planktonic conditions than those evolved planktonically [MIC = 0.58 mg/L (SEM = 0.13) vs. MIC = 8.53 mg/L (SEM = 1.96), two-tailed t-test: p<0.05, t = 4.048, df = 80].
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Biofilm-evolved clones were more fit relative to the ancestral strain than the planktonic-evolved clones in the absence of antibiotic.
source: However, biofilm-evolved clones were more fit relative to the ancestral strain than the planktonic-evolved clones in the absence of antibiotic (two-tailed t-test: p=0.008, t = 2.984 df=18) (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: One planktonic-evolved clone with mutations in both gyrA and parC exhibited no significant fitness cost and high levels of resistance.
source: However, one planktonic-evolved clone with mutations in both gyrA and parC exhibited no significant fitness cost and high levels of resistance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The parC mutation may compensate for the cost imposed by the gyrA mutation.
source: This suggests that, as in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, the parC mutation may compensate for the cost imposed by the gyrA mutation (Kugelberg et al., 2005), an example of sign epistasis (Sackman and Rokyta, 2018).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: Mutants selected in biofilm-evolved populations were less resistant than mutants selected in planktonic populations but produced more biofilm and paid little or no fitness cost in the absence of antibiotics.
source: Overall, mutants selected in biofilm-evolved populations were less resistant than mutants selected in planktonic populations (Figure 1B) but produced more biofilm (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and paid little or no fitness cost in the absence of antibiotics (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Cost-free resistance implies that these subpopulations could persist in the absence of drug, limiting the treatment options.
source: This cost-free resistance implies that these subpopulations could persist in the absence of drug, limiting the treatment options and demanding new approaches to treat high fitness, resistant pathogens (Baym et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: Changes in susceptibilities to 13 antibiotics were observed that depended upon the growth mode of prior selection.
source: Changes in susceptibilities were observed in 13 antibiotics that depended upon the growth mode of prior selection (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Planktonic-evolved populations exhibited cross resistance to cefpodoxime and ceftazidime.
source: For example, planktonic-evolved populations exhibited cross resistance to cefpodoxime and ceftazidime
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Biofilm-evolved populations evolved collateral sensitivity to cefpodoxime and ceftazidime.
source: but biofilm-evolved populations evolved collateral sensitivity to these cephalosporins
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Cross-resistance was associated genetically with adeN, adeS, gyrA or pgpB mutations.
source: Cross-resistance was associated genetically with adeN, adeS, gyrA or pgpB mutations
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: Collateral sensitivity was associated with adeL mutations.
source: and collateral sensitivity was associated with adeL mutations
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic sequencing data.

claim: Each RND efflux pump is suggested to be specific for certain classes of antibiotics.
source: In A. baumannii, each RND efflux pump is suggested to be specific for certain classes of antibiotics (Table 4) (Coyne et al., 2011; Li et al., 2016; Leus et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and a table.

claim: Efflux pumps AdeABC and AdeIJK increased the resistance level to some β-lactams when overexpressed.
source: Similar to our results (Figure 4), Yoon and collaborators demonstrated that efflux pumps AdeABC and AdeIJK, regulated by adeS and adeN respectively, increased the resistance level to some β-lactams when overexpressed (Yoon et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and comparison to experimental data.

claim: Production of AdeFGH decreased resistance to some β-lactams and other families of antibiotics or detergents by an unknown mechanism.
source: However, production of AdeFGH, the efflux pump regulated by adeL, decreased resistance to some β-lactams and other families of antibiotics or detergents by an unknown mechanism (Yoon et al., 2015; Leus et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Increased sensitivity to β-lactams with efflux overexpression has also been reported in P. aeruginosa.
source: Increased sensitivity to β-lactams with efflux overexpression has also been reported in P. aeruginosa (Azimi and Rastegar Lari, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Exploiting collateral sensitivity has been proposed to counteract the evolution of resistant populations both in bacteria and in cancer.
source: Exploiting collateral sensitivity has been proposed to counteract the evolution of resistant populations both in bacteria (Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Kim et al., 2014; Nichol et al., 2019) and in cancer (Dhawan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Biofilm growth may generate collateral sensitivity during treatment with CIP and potentially other fluoroquinolones.
source: Remarkably, our results show that biofilm growth, commonly thought to broaden resistance, may actually generate collateral sensitivity during treatment with CIP and potentially other fluoroquinolones.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Experimental evolution is a powerful method of screening naturally arising genetic variation for mutants that are the best fit in a defined condition.
source: Experimental evolution is a powerful method of screening naturally arising genetic variation for mutants that are the best fit in a defined condition (Elena and Lenski, 2003; Cooper, 2018; Van den Bergh et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The probability that every site in the A. baumannii genome experiences a mutation at least once over the course of the 12 day experiment is very likely.
source: When population sizes are large and reproductive rates are rapid, as they were here, the probability that all possible single-step mutations that can increase both resistance and fitness occurred in each population is very likely.
evidence: This is an inference based on population genetics calculations.

claim: S81L in gyrA and S80L in parC have been reported worldwide as the primary mechanism conferring high levels of resistance to fluroquinolones in clinical isolates.
source: For instance, S81L in gyrA and S80L in parC have been reported worldwide as the primary mechanism conferring high levels of resistance to fluroquinolones in clinical isolates (Adams-Haduch et al., 2008; Warner et al., 2016; Dahdouh et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in RND efflux pumps have been associated with multidrug resistant phenotypes in clinical samples isolated worldwide.
source: and mutations in RND efflux pumps have been associated with multidrug resistant phenotypes in clinical samples isolated worldwide (Damier-Piolle et al., 2008; Coyne et al., 2010; Rosenfeld et al., 2012; Fernando et al., 2013; Pournaras et al., 2016; Leus et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Evolution experiments hold promise for ultimately forecasting mutations selected by different antimicrobials and anticipating treatment outcomes.
source: Evolution experiments hold promise for ultimately forecasting mutations selected by different antimicrobials and anticipating treatment outcomes, including the diversification of the pathogen population and the likelihood of collateral sensitivity or cross-resistance (Brockhurst et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Knowledge of the prevailing lifestyle of the pathogen population may be critically important for treatment design.
source: Furthermore, knowledge of the prevailing lifestyle of the pathogen population may be critically important for treatment design.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Biofilm-forming clinical isolates were more susceptible to CIP and other antibiotics than non-biofilm forming clinical isolates even when the resistance levels were measured in biofilms.
source: As predicted by our experiment, biofilm-forming clinical isolates were more susceptible to CIP and other antibiotics than non-biofilm forming clinical isolates even when the resistance levels were measured in biofilms (Rodríguez-Baño et al., 2008; Qi et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Most infections are likely caused by surface-attached populations.
source: Most infections are likely caused by surface-attached populations (Wolcott et al., 2010; Wolcott, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Tobramycin is used for treating P. aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis patients.
source: For example, tobramycin is used for treating P. aeruginosa in cystic fibrosis patients (Hamed and Debonnett, 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Tobramycin promotes biofilm formation.
source: and promotes biofilm formation (Hoffman et al., 2005; Linares et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The overexpression of RND efflux pumps in both P. aeruginosa and Neisseria gonorrhoeae may produce little or no fitness cost.
source: As in our experiment, the overexpression of RND efflux pumps in both P. aeruginosa and Neisseria gonorrhoeae may produce little or no fitness cost (Warner et al., 2007; Olivares Pacheco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Conventional wisdom has long held that the relationship between resistance and fitness is antagonistic.
source: Broader still, conventional wisdom has long held that the relationship between resistance and fitness is antagonistic, and that the efficacy of many antimicrobials is aided by a severe fitness cost of resistance (Vogwill and MacLean, 2015; Baym et al., 2016b; Hughes and Andersson, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The form of the relationship between fitness and resistance can be altered by the mode of growth, whereby biofilms can align resistance and fitness traits.
source: This study demonstrates that the form of the relationship between fitness and resistance can be altered by the mode of growth, whereby biofilms can align resistance and fitness traits.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Both evolutionary dynamics and the identities of mutations differed between lifestyle.
source: Both evolutionary dynamics and the identities of mutations differed between lifestyle.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Planktonic populations experienced selective sweeps of mutations including the primary topoisomerase drug targets.
source: Planktonic populations experienced selective sweeps of mutations including the primary topoisomerase drug targets
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Biofilm-adapted populations acquired mutations in regulators of efflux pumps.
source: whereas biofilm-adapted populations acquired mutations in regulators of efflux pumps
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: An overall trade-off between fitness and resistance level emerged, wherein biofilm-adapted clones were less resistant than planktonic but more fit in the absence of drug.
source: An overall trade-off between fitness and resistance level emerged, wherein biofilm-adapted clones were less resistant than planktonic but more fit in the absence of drug.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: Biofilm populations developed collateral sensitivity to cephalosporins.
source: However, biofilm populations developed collateral sensitivity to cephalosporins, demonstrating the clinical relevance of lifestyle on the evolution of resistance.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: The transfer population size in biofilm and in planktonic cultures was set to be nearly equivalent at the beginning of the experiment at approximately 1 × 10^7 CFU/mL.
source: The transfer population size in biofilm and in planktonic cultures was set to be nearly equivalent at the beginning of the experiment (approximately 1 × 107 CFU/mL), because population size influences mutation availability and the response to selection (Salverda et al., 2017; Cooper, 2018).
evidence: This describes a methodological decision supported by citations.

claim: Each day, the population size increases 100-fold during regrowth, generating approximately 10^6 new mutations per day using a conservative but experimentally justified estimate of the mutation rate.
source: Each day, the population size increases 100-fold during regrowth, generating approximately 106 new mutations per day using a conservative but experimentally justified estimate of the mutation rate (Lynch et al., 2016; Dillon et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a calculation based on experimental parameters and citations.

claim: Effects of fluoroquinolones like CIP have been shown to increase the mutation rate by an order of magnitude.
source: Effects of fluoroquinolones like CIP have been shown to increase the mutation rate by an order of magnitude, and some studies suggest biofilm growth may also increase the mutation rate (Boles and Singh, 2008; Long et al., 2016; Pribis et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Biofilm clones produced more biofilm than planktonic clones.
source: Biofilm clones produced more biofilm than planktonic clones: two tailed t-test of biofilm formation with 0.00 mg/L of CIP: p=0.006, t = 3.008, df = 32; with 0.01 mg/L of CIP: p=0.0006, t = 3.780, df = 32; with 0.03 mg/L of CIP: p=0.0077 t=2.841, df = 32 and with 0.0625 mg/L of CIP: p=0.018 t=2.471 df=32.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.
